title: A hymn in Majh
hookLine: Majh holds Guru Arjan's letters and the Barah Maha

cards: A moment, and a year. One is a single moment of missing someone; the other is a whole year coming back around. Raga Majh holds a hymn of each, and Guru Arjan wrote both.
One is a set of letters from a son far from his father. The other walks through the twelve months, one by one. Year two read each on its own.
Today, side by side, in the raga they share.

teach.h: THE LETTERS: A MOMENT IS AN AGE.
teach.b: First, the letters. Tradition says young Arjan was sent to Lahore by his father, Guru Ram Das, and told to stay until he was called. The call didn't come, and he wrote home in verse.
In the Granth the verses stand as one shabad in Majh. My mind longs for a sight of the Guru, the first stanza says in effect; it cries like the rainbird for rain.
In the third, the longing is measured in a single moment: when I can't meet you for even a moment, it's a dark age for me. A moment, stretched into an age.
Then the Barah Maha, the song of the twelve months, also in Majh, also Guru Arjan's. Its months begin with Chet: in Chet, it says in paraphrase, remember the Lord of the world, and a deep joy comes.

teach.h: THE BARAH MAHA: MONTH AFTER MONTH.
teach.b: Month follows month, and each asks the same thing of the soul, the bride waiting for her Lord: is this the month we meet? Here the longing is measured in months, the whole turning year.
Hear the two together and Majh makes sense. One counts moments, the other months. Both are about distance from the beloved, and both end by finding him near.
The letters close with the Lord found in the singer's own home.
The months close by saying that months, days and moments are blessed for the one the Lord looks on with grace.
The raga's homesick sound fits both. Tomorrow, a raga whose section runs on for page after page.

how: Guru Arjan's shabad of the letters is sung in kirtan in Raag Majh, and the Barah Maha in Majh is read in some gurdwaras at the start of each month of the Indian calendar, on Sangrand.

games.q: what does “a hymn in majh” mean?
o: a hymn of thanks for a good harvest
Guru Arjan's longing, in moments and in months
Guru Nanak's letters home from his travels

games.q: two hymns in Majh — tap the pairs.
p: a son far from his father
the twelve months, one by one
remember the Lord, and joy comes

s: the letters and the Barah Maha are in different ragas
both are in Majh, and both are Guru Arjan's.
in the letters, the rainbird cries for rain
the mind longs for the Guru's sight like the rainbird for rain.
the Barah Maha's months begin in winter

games.q: you're setting two hymns of longing, one measured in moments, one in months. which raga do you give them?
o: two different ragas, to keep them apart.
the same raga, Majh, with its sound of missing.
no raga, so the words stand alone.
games.why: both stand in Majh, so the same homesick sound carries the son's letters and the soul's year of waiting.

practice: If you can, let a recording of Guru Arjan's letters, or the Barah Maha in Majh, play through the sit, listening for where the voice reaches and where it rests.

Otherwise, try longing's two scales: first a moment, one person you'd like to see today, then a year, one thing you've waited for since last spring, holding each for a few breaths without fixing anything.
If you pray, let Waheguru be the word that answers both.

wordCard.voice: A hymn in Majh. Guru Arjan's letters, where a moment apart is an age, and his Barah Maha, where the months pass in waiting, two shapes of longing in one raga. Today's word.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: the twelve months, Guru Arjan's song of the year in Raag Majh.

carryVoice: Your line: letters of longing. A moment or a year, both end with the beloved near. I'll be here tomorrow.
